text.en:
In an ancient city the potter, the blacksmith, the weaver and the trader all had their own streets. Farmers brought grain in carts to the market.
A royal officer collected a share of the produce as tax.
"A city needs many kinds of workers," said the guide.

After the Indus cities declined, new villages and cities grew in the Ganga plains from about 3000 years ago. Iron tools helped farmers clear forests and grow more food.
The more food people grew, the more crafts, trade and cities developed. Rulers collected taxes and kept armies. Some small kingdoms joined to form larger states called Mahajanapadas, such as Magadha, Kosala and Vatsa.
Magadha became powerful because of its fertile land, iron mines and rivers for travel and trade. Rajagriha and later Pataliputra were its capitals.

problem.en: Why did Magadha become so powerful?

text.en: It had fertile land, so it could grow plenty of food.
It had iron mines for tools and weapons.
And rivers helped trade and travel. So it grew strong.

prompt.en: A friend says kings did not take taxes. How will you explain?

requiredIdeas.en: Rulers collected a share of produce and money as tax.
This paid for armies, roads and officials.

commonMisconceptions.en: Assuming no taxes existed in ancient times.

points.en: New cities grew in the Ganga plains with iron tools.
Magadha was strong because of land, iron and rivers.
